newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka Tamil parties urge end to ethnic crisis.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka Tamil parties urge end to ethnic crisis.

text.p: Sri Lanka's Tamil political parties are getting edgy over a delay in introducing changes to the constitution to give wide autonomy to minorities aimed at ending the country's ethnic crisis.

Tamil politicians said on Sunday the government had been dragging its feet over a draft constitution being discussed in a parliamentary select committee and that further delay might lead to an intensification of the war that has already killed thousands.
Murugesu Sivasithambaram, leader of the mainline Tamil United Liberation Front (TULF), told Reuters on Sunday his party was upset with the government over its inability to end the conflict quickly.
"We are stressing the need for a ceasefire and start of negotiations (with the rebels) for the settlement of the northeast problem," he said.
Sivasithambaram said his party was planning to walk out of parliament when the house debates emergency laws next month as a protest against the government's handling of the conflict.
"This will be a demonstration that we are dissatisfied with the way the government is handling the situation," he said.

Sri Lanka is ravaged by a war, now in its 14th year, waged by Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) rebels against government troops. The LTTE demand an independent homeland for minority Tamils in the Indian Ocean island's north and east.
The government says more than 50,000 people have been killed in the war. The LTTE say the toll is higher.

Negotiations in the committee on key issues like devolution of power to minorities and demarcation of proposed new councils, have become stuck due to disagreements between Tamil and Moslem parties, and between the main opposition United National Party (UNP) and the government.
TULF officials said the party had resolved at a recent meeting to call upon both the government and the LTTE to stop fighting and initiate third party mediation for a negotiated settlement.
Other Tamil political parties have written to both the ruling People's Alliance (PA) and the UNP expressing dissatisfaction over their inability to find a solution to the conflict.
An agreement in March between the PA and the UNP to work together to end the conflict had raised hopes of a quick resolution of the problem. But since then little has happened.
Former rebel Douglas Devananda, leader of the Eelam People's Democratic Party (EPDP), told Reuters the letter was aimed at pushing the government to expedite the political package.
"I can't see any reasons why it is being delayed. But we need the political package before we start negotiating with the LTTE," Devananda said.
The government, which unveiled parts of the new constitution in March, has said it proposes to complete the draft before the parliament's budget session in November.

Sivasithambarama said his party had been assured by the government that the draft constitution would be ready before the budget session, but added that if there was a further delay his party would be forced to consider other political options.
